```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import polars as pl
import hubbub as hb

out_dir = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="hubbub-gifs-"))


def show_gif(path):
    """Embed a GIF in the page so it survives rebuilds and the freeze cache."""
    import base64

    data = base64.b64encode(Path(path).read_bytes()).decode()
    print(f'<img src="data:image/gif;base64,{data}" style="width:100%">')
```

On this page I'll build the charts and GIFs for my own profile README ([mjfrigaard/mjfrigaard](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/mjfrigaard)) with `hubbub`. We'll pull my GitHub activity, take a look at it, chart it a few ways, and then animate three of the charts.

## Collect the data

`collect_git_commits()` calls the GitHub API, so set a token first (`export GITHUB_PAT=$(gh auth token)` works if you use the GitHub CLI). Asking for all four types returns a dict of DataFrames:

```python
stats = hb.collect_git_commits(
    user="mjfrigaard",
    emails=["you@example.com", "you@work.example.com"],
    include=["commits", "stars", "issues", "prs"],
    tz="America/Phoenix",
)
for name, df in stats.items():
    df.write_parquet(f"data/{name}.parquet")
```

The `emails` filter keeps only commits I authored, and `tz` sets the time zone for the `local_ts`, `date`, `hour`, `weekday`, and `year` columns. Pulling every commit from every repo takes a few hundred API calls, so I saved the results to parquet files and read them back here:

```{python}
#| label: read
stats = {
    name: pl.read_parquet(f"data/{name}.parquet")
    for name in ["commits", "stars", "issues", "prs"]
}
commits = stats["commits"]
{name: df.shape for name, df in stats.items()}
```

## A first look

Each row in `commits` is one commit:

```{python}
#| label: glimpse
commits.select("repo", "local_ts", "date", "hour", "weekday", "year").tail(5)
```

Which repos have the most commits?

```{python}
#| label: top-repos
(
    commits.group_by("repo")
    .agg(commits=pl.len(), first=pl.col("date").min(), last=pl.col("date").max())
    .sort("commits", descending=True)
    .head(8)
)
```

And which of my repos have the most stars?

```{python}
#| label: stars
stats["stars"].select("repo", "stargazers_count", "language").head(5)
```

The `issues` and `prs` tables cover everything I've opened across GitHub, not only in my own repos:

```{python}
#| label: prs
(
    stats["prs"]
    .with_columns(owner=pl.col("repo").str.split("/").list.first())
    .group_by("owner", "state")
    .agg(prs=pl.len())
    .sort("prs", descending=True)
)
```

## Charts

Every chart function takes the commits DataFrame plus optional `repo`, `date_begin`, and `date_end` filters, and returns a matplotlib `Figure`.

### Calendar heatmap

`calendar_heatmap_plot()` draws the familiar GitHub grid with one row per year:

```{python}
#| label: calendar
#| fig-width: 11
hb.calendar_heatmap_plot(commits, date_begin="2023-01-01");
```

### Cumulative commits

`cumulative_line_plot()` keeps the `top_n` busiest repos as their own lines and rolls the rest into "Other":

```{python}
#| label: cumulative
hb.cumulative_line_plot(commits, date_begin="2023-01-01", top_n=8);
```

### Punchcard

`punchcard_plot()` shows when I commit, by weekday and hour (in Phoenix time):

```{python}
#| label: punchcard
hb.punchcard_plot(commits, date_begin="2023-01-01");
```

### Scatter with densities

`scatter_density_plot()` plots any two of `"repo"`, `"time"`, `"date"`, and `"weekday"`. The `"density"` type adds marginal density curves:

```{python}
#| label: scatter-density
hb.scatter_density_plot(
    commits, date_begin="2025-01-01", x="date", y="time", plot_type="density"
);
```

Set `plot_type="plotly"` for an interactive version you can hover over:

```{python}
#| label: scatter-plotly
hb.scatter_density_plot(
    commits, date_begin="2025-01-01", x="weekday", y="time", plot_type="plotly"
)
```

### Spirals

The spiral charts make one turn per year, starting in the center, with January at the top. Each one shows the same daily counts a different way:

```{python}
#| label: spiral-heatmap
hb.spiral_heatmap_plot(commits, date_begin="2020-01-01");
```

```{python}
#| label: spiral-points
hb.spiral_points_plot(commits, date_begin="2020-01-01");
```

```{python}
#| label: spiral-horizon
hb.spiral_horizon_plot(commits, date_begin="2020-01-01");
```

### Interactive spiral

Every spiral function also takes `plot_type="plotly"`. Hover over a bar to see the date and commit count, click a band in the legend to hide it, and drag to zoom:

```{python}
#| label: spiral-plotly
hb.spiral_horizon_plot(commits, date_begin="2020-01-01", plot_type="plotly")
```

GitHub strips JavaScript from READMEs, so my profile shows a static copy of this chart that links here:

```python
fig = hb.spiral_horizon_plot(commits, date_begin="2020-01-01")
fig.savefig("spiral.png", dpi=96, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor="white")
```

## Animate the charts

A GIF is a stack of frames. Each recipe below saves one chart per frame to a temporary folder, then `make_gif()` assembles them. Close each figure after saving it so they don't pile up in memory.

### Recipe 1: cumulative commits, sliding the end date

```{python}
#| label: gif-cumulative
#| output: asis
from datetime import date

ends = pl.date_range(
    date(2023, 2, 1), commits["date"].max(), interval="1mo", eager=True
)
frames = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
for i, end in enumerate(ends, start=1):
    fig = hb.cumulative_line_plot(
        commits, date_begin="2023-01-01", date_end=end, top_n=8
    )
    fig.set_size_inches(10, 6)
    fig.savefig(frames / f"{i:04d}.png", dpi=96, facecolor="white")
    plt.close(fig)

gif = hb.make_gif(frames, out_dir / "cumulative.gif", width=1000, height=600,
                  first_duration=1, frame_duration=0.4, last_duration=4)
show_gif(gif)
```

### Recipe 2: calendar heatmap, year by year

```{python}
#| label: gif-calendar
#| output: asis
years = sorted(commits.filter(pl.col("year") >= 2023)["year"].unique())
frames = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
for i, yr in enumerate(years, start=1):
    fig = hb.calendar_heatmap_plot(
        commits, date_begin=f"{years[0]}-01-01", date_end=f"{yr}-12-31",
        title=f"Through {yr}",
    )
    fig.set_size_inches(11, 7)
    fig.savefig(frames / f"{i:04d}.png", dpi=96, facecolor="white")
    plt.close(fig)

gif = hb.make_gif(frames, out_dir / "calendar.gif", width=1100, height=700,
                  first_duration=1, frame_duration=1.2, last_duration=4)
show_gif(gif)
```

### Recipe 3: a punchcard for each top repo

```{python}
#| label: gif-punchcard
#| output: asis
top_repos = (
    commits.group_by("repo").agg(n=pl.len())
    .sort("n", descending=True)["repo"].head(6).to_list()
)
frames = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
for i, repo in enumerate(top_repos, start=1):
    fig = hb.punchcard_plot(commits, repo=repo)
    fig.set_size_inches(10, 5)
    fig.savefig(frames / f"{i:04d}.png", dpi=96, facecolor="white")
    plt.close(fig)

gif = hb.make_gif(frames, out_dir / "punchcard.gif", width=1000, height=500,
                  first_duration=1, frame_duration=1.5, last_duration=4)
show_gif(gif)
```

To rank repos by stars instead, use `stats["stars"]["repo"].head(6)`.

### The introduction

```{python}
#| label: gif-intro
#| output: asis
gif = hb.who_am_i_gif(
    name="Martin",
    likes="#rstats and data visualization.",
    learn="Shiny for Python app development and Linux administration.",
    work="Shiny app-package development tools.",
    collab="#rstats and #pystats packages for data science.",
    output=out_dir / "who_am_i.gif",
)
show_gif(gif)
```

## Put it in the README

In the profile repo, save the GIFs next to `README.md` and point to them from `build_readme.py`:

```python
sections = [
    "# Hi there 👋",
    "![](who_am_i.gif)",
    "## GitHub activity",
    "![Cumulative commits](cumulative.gif)",
    "![Calendar heatmap](calendar.gif)",
    "![Punchcard](punchcard.gif)",
    hb.gh_badges("mjfrigaard", ["details", "stats", "repo_lang"], theme="dark"),
]
Path("README.md").write_text("\n\n".join(sections) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
```
